hints: Focus on the thermal decomposition pattern for Group 2 nitrates, which always gives a metal oxide solid plus nitrogen dioxide and oxygen as gases.
Work out that 1 mole of any Group 2 nitrate, $\text{M(NO}_3)_2$, always releases the same mass of gas, $4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$, which is 108 g.
Use the mass ratio from the experiment, 1.32 g gas from 2.00 g solid, to find the $M_r$ of the nitrate and then subtract 124 to identify the metal.
walkthrough:
**Write the common decomposition equation**

All Group 2 nitrates decompose in the same way to the oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen. Only the oxide stays as a solid.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$2\text{M(NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{MO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$

**Find the mass of gas from one mole of nitrate**

From the equation, 2 moles of nitrate give 4 moles of $\text{NO}_2$ and 1 mole of $\text{O}_2$. Divide by 2 for 1 mole.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$m_{gas \text{ per mole}} = \frac{4 \times 46.0 + 32.0}{2} = \frac{216.0}{2} = 108.0 \text{ g}$$

**Link the experimental masses to $M_r$**

The fraction of mass lost as gas must equal 108.0 divided by the $M_r$ of the nitrate. We know this fraction from the data.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\frac{108.0}{M_r[\text{M(NO}_3)_2]} = \frac{1.32}{2.00} = 0.66$$
$$M_r[\text{M(NO}_3)_2] = \frac{108.0}{0.66} \approx 163.6$$

**Identify the metal**

Each nitrate is $\text{M(NO}_3)_2$, so $M_r = A_r(\text{M}) + 2 \times 62.0 = A_r(\text{M}) + 124.0$. Subtract to find the metal.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$A_r(\text{M}) \approx 163.6 - 124.0 \approx 39.6$$
This is very close to calcium, $A_r \approx 40.1$, so the salt is calcium nitrate.

options.A: Incorrect. Beryllium is very light ($A_r \approx 9.0$), so $M_r \approx 133.1$. The gas fraction would be $108.0/133.1 \approx 0.81$, giving about 1.62 g of gas from 2.00 g, much more than 1.32 g.
options.B: Correct. Calcium nitrate has $M_r \approx 40.1 + 124.0 = 164.1$. The expected gas mass is $2.00 \times 108.0/164.1 \approx 1.32$ g, which matches the data exactly.
options.C: Incorrect. Magnesium nitrate has $M_r \approx 24.3 + 124.0 = 148.3$. The expected gas mass is $2.00 \times 108.0/148.3 \approx 1.46$ g, which is larger than 1.32 g because magnesium is lighter than calcium.
options.D: Incorrect. Strontium is heavy ($A_r \approx 87.6$), so $M_r \approx 211.6$. The gas fraction would be $108.0/211.6 \approx 0.51$, giving only about 1.02 g of gas from 2.00 g, less than observed.
